entries.name: Black pepper
entries.spread: Middle East and Rome as early as the 1st century BCE; Vietnam now dominates production
needs: support trees or poles for the vine
entries.notes: The single most traded spice; Roman demand paid for much of the India trade. Vietnam, India and Indonesia grow most of it today.

entries.name: Cinnamon (true cinnamon)
entries.spread: Known to Pharaonic Egypt and classical Rome; Sri Lanka held the monopoly until Dutch and British planters
needs: young stems harvested for the bark
entries.notes: The inner bark of a small tree; much 'cinnamon' sold today is the related cassia. Ceylon cinnamon is milder and flakier.

entries.name: Clove
entries.spread: Syria and Mesopotamia by 1700 BCE; Arab trade to China; Dutch monopoly in the 17th century
entries.notes: Flower buds dried whole. Once worth its weight in silver; the Banda and Ternate nutmeg/clove monopolies drove the spice age.

entries.name: Nutmeg and mace
entries.spread: China knew it by the 1st-2nd century; reached Europe via the Arab trade in the Middle Ages
needs: long maturation, first crop after ~7 years
entries.notes: One fruit gives two spices: the seed (nutmeg) and its red aril (mace). The sole source was the tiny Banda Islands until the 18th century.

entries.name: Saffron
entries.spread: Crete and Minoan trade ~1700 BCE; spread across the Mediterranean and Persia; Iran, Spain and India today lead
needs: dry hot summer and cool winter
harvested by hand over two weeks
entries.notes: Sterile triploid that propagates only by corm; roughly 150,000 flowers for one kilogram of stigmas. The most expensive spice by weight, affordable only because labour is cheap.

entries.name: Vanilla
entries.wild_ancestor: wild Vanilla planifolia (Gulf of Mexico lowlands)
entries.spread: Introduced to Europe in the 1520s; Bourbon islands (Reunion, Madagascar) produce most of it since the 19th century
needs: hand pollination outside its native range
entries.notes: A climbing orchid; every vanilla outside Mesoamerica is hand-pollinated. Cured pods develop their aroma only through a months-long sweating and drying process.

entries.name: Cardamom (green cardamom)
entries.spread: Ancient Arab and Greek trade; Guatemala, not India, is the top exporter since the early 20th century
needs: deep shade and very high humidity
rich well-drained soil with leaf litter
entries.notes: A ginger-family understorey plant picked at the capsule stage and sun- or fire-dried. Third most expensive spice after saffron and vanilla.

entries.name: Ginger
entries.spread: India and China since antiquity; Arab traders to Rome; Spanish galleons carried it to the Caribbean; now grown worldwide
needs: rhizomes planted whole, harvested before frost
entries.notes: Grown from rhizome cuttings; no wild ancestor has been identified. One of the few spices that is also eaten as a vegetable.

entries.name: Turmeric
entries.spread: Throughout premodern Asia as dye, medicine and food; Dutch traders carried it to Europe in the 17th century
needs: rhizomes lifted, boiled, dried and polished
entries.notes: The golden dye and curry staple; curcumin gives it colour and most of its medicinal reputation. Central to South and Southeast Asian cuisines.

entries.name: Chilli pepper
entries.spread: Iberia and the Columbian exchange; India, Sichuan and Thailand built cuisines around it within two centuries of 1500
needs: regular harvest to keep plants bearing
entries.notes: A New World spice that rewrote Asian and European cooking after 1492. Capsaicin deters mammals but not birds, which spread the seed.

entries.name: Allspice
entries.wild_ancestor: wild Pimenta dioica (Mexico to Central America)

domesticated.where: Mesoamerica; Jamaica is the leading producer

entries.spread: Spanish captured the plant from Mesoamerican use; Jamaica monopolised trade from the 17th century
needs: picked as near-ripe berries, then dried
entries.notes: Dried unripe berries taste of clove, cinnamon and nutmeg combined; the Mayans likely cultivated it. Native to one small region of the Americas.

entries.name: Star anise
entries.wild_ancestor: wild Illicium verum (south China, northern Vietnam)
entries.spread: Staple of Chinese 'five-spice'; European trade from the 16th century; now a key feedstock for oseltamivir (Tamiflu)
entries.notes: A small evergreen tree; the fruit is a woody eight-pointed star. Frequent confusion with highly toxic Japanese star anise (I. anisatum) is a real hazard.

entries.name: Cumin
entries.spread: Egypt under the pharaohs; Rome and the Islamic world; India is now the largest grower
entries.notes: A small umbellifer grown for its seed. One of the oldest documented spices and central to Indian, Mexican and Middle Eastern cooking.

entries.name: Coriander
entries.spread: Neolithic sites in Europe and India; grown by Rome; now global, from Russia to Morocco to Mexico
needs: swift to bolt; succession sowings keep leaves coming
entries.notes: Leaves (cilantro) and seeds are two different spices from one plant. Genetics, not upbringing, decides whether cilantro tastes of soap.

entries.name: Fennel (seed)
entries.spread: Ancient Greece and Rome; carried by Rome to Britain and by Islamic traders eastward
entries.notes: The bulb vegetable and the seed spice are forms of one species. Sweet, aniseed-like seed; a classic digestive chew after meals in India.

entries.name: Caraway
entries.spread: Known in Stone Age Europe; Roman and medieval Europe; still the signature spice of rye bread in northern and eastern Europe
needs: biennial: flowers in year two, then dies
entries.notes: A biennial umbellifer domesticated in prehistoric Europe; its seed flavours rye bread, sauerkraut and European cheeses.

entries.name: Anise
entries.spread: Egypt, Greece and Rome; backbone of ouzo, rakı and sambuca; Mughal India took it as a breath freshener and digestive
entries.notes: Not the same plant as star anise; both smell of anethole but are unrelated. Old medicinal standby for colic and coughs.

entries.name: White mustard
entries.spread: Ancient Rome and Egypt; Dijon mustard in medieval France; global condiment crop today
needs: any decent soil; fast cover crop too
entries.notes: Also grown as a green manure. The hot bite comes from sinigrin, activated only when the seed is ground and wetted.

entries.name: Galangal (greater)
entries.spread: Throughout maritime and mainland Southeast Asia; central flavour of tom yum; reached Europe in the Middle Ages as a medicine
entries.notes: A rhizome spice like ginger but piney and medicinal. Greater galangal dominates Thai and Indonesian cooking; lesser galangal dominates Southeast Asia proper.

entries.name: Asafoetida
entries.spread: Silk Road trade to Rome; almost unknown in Europe today except in Indian-diaspora food and 'hing' in curries
needs: resin tapped from the living taproot
entries.notes: Dried latex resin famous for smelling of garlic and onion; a pinch sized for a witch's cauldron. Long used as a digestive and anti-flatulent.

entries.name: Sichuan pepper
entries.spread: Core of Sichuan cuisine; banned from US imports 1968-2005 due to citrus canker fears
needs: harvested as rinds once the pods split
entries.notes: A citrus relative whose rind carries hydroxy-alpha-sanshool, a molecule that makes lips tingle and buzz. The defining 'ma' of Sichuan pepper.

entries.name: Grains of paradise
entries.spread: Medieval Europe's pepper; Portuguese West African trade; nearly forgotten until craft brewers revived it
entries.notes: A ginger-family pod spice prized in 14th-century Europe before black pepper undercut it. Famous among brewers of farmhouse ales and saisons.

entries.name: Opium poppy
entries.spread: Neolithic Europe and the Near East; Islamic Golden Age pharmacology; Bengal opium financed British India and triggered the Opium Wars
entries.notes: Also grown for seed, oil and pharmaceutical morphine. The single plant behind most of the world's opioid supply, legal and otherwise.

entries.name: Coca
entries.wild_ancestor: wild Erythroxylum gracilipes (eastern Andes / upper Amazon)
entries.spread: Sacred to the Inca; chewing persists across the Andes; cocaine isolation in the 1850s industrialised it; Colombian cartels and coca leaf cola share one plant
needs: warm moist inter-Andean valleys and eastern slopes
entries.notes: Chewed with lime for altitude and fatigue for millennia; now the engine of a global illicit trade. The flavour of Coca-Cola still requires coca leaf from Peru.

entries.name: Cannabis
entries.spread: Fiber and rope from Scythia to China; written about by Herodotus; Islamic, Indian and Taoist use; global in both legal and illicit markets today
needs: long frost-free season; short-day to flower
entries.notes: First domesticated for fibre, seed and medicine before recreational use. THC and CBD profiles are now bred for divergent markets; hemp and marijuana are the same species.

entries.name: Tobacco
entries.wild_ancestor: hybrid of Nicotiana sylvestris and N. tomentosiformis (South America)
entries.spread: Spread across the Americas pre-Columbian; to Europe within a decade of 1492; a fixture of colonial Virginia and Spanish Cuba within a century
needs: shade-grown leaves for cigars; sun-grown for Virginia leaf
entries.notes: A plant no human ever ate; smoked, chewed and snuffed. Once a colonial currency, now among the leading preventable causes of death worldwide.

entries.name: Tea
entries.spread: China for millennia; Japan c. 800 CE; Dutch East India Company to Europe; British plantations in Assam and Ceylon undercut China's monopoly in the 19th century
needs: picked as bud and two young leaves
entries.notes: The world's most consumed psychoactive drink after water rules it. All true teas are one species; processing, not plant, makes green, oolong, black and pu-erh.

entries.name: Coffee (Arabica)
entries.wild_ancestor: natural hybrid Coffea eugenioides and Coffea canephora (Ethiopian highlands)
entries.spread: Sufi monks and Yemen's port of Mocha; Ottoman coffeehouses; Dutch to Java; French to the Caribbean; now Brazil and Vietnam dominate volume
needs: frost-free tropics at 600-2000 m altitude for Arabica
entries.notes: Arabica is half the market and the finer cup; Robusta the rest. The second-most-traded commodity on Earth by value after crude oil, depending on the year.

entries.name: Cacao
entries.spread: Ecuador to Mesoamerica; Aztec and Maya ritual drink; Spanish court in the 1520s; Africa supplies over 70% of beans today
needs: deep shade under plantain or forest
entries.notes: The bitter bean behind chocolate; fermentation is what turns it from sour pulp-seed into cocoa flavour. Domestication is far older than Mesoamerica.

entries.name: Kava
entries.spread: Ancestral across Melanesia and Polynesia; central to Pacific social life and ceremony; exported to the diaspora and alternative-wellness markets
needs: 4+ years to first harvest; propagated by stem cuttings only
entries.notes: A sterile clone that exists only because humans keep planting it. Kavalactones bring calm without intoxication; the Pacific drink is the ice-breaker of every village meeting.

entries.name: Betel
entries.spread: Chewed across the Indian Ocean and Pacific Rim for millennia; a daily ritual from Mumbai to Jakarta to Port Moresby
needs: needs areca palm nut and slaked lime to be chewed as quid
entries.notes: The leaf itself is chewed with areca nut and lime paste; it stains teeth black-red. Hundreds of millions chew it daily - one of the most common psychoactive habits on Earth.

entries.name: Ephedra (ma huang)
entries.spread: Central to Chinese materia medica for five millennia; ephedrine isolated in 1929; source of modern decongestants and a banned diet-pill era
entries.notes: The original source of ephedrine, a powerful bronchodilator and CNS stimulant. Ephedrine-based weight loss products were pulled from most Western markets in the 2000s.

entries.name: Cinchona
entries.wild_ancestor: wild Cinchona spp. (eastern Andes, Peru and Ecuador)

domesticated.where: Andes; plantation-grown in Java and India from the 19th century

entries.spread: Jesuit use from the 1630s; Dutch plantations in Java broke the Andean monopoly; first synthetic antimalarials arrived in the 1930s-40s
needs: bark stripped from trunk or root, then dried
entries.notes: The bark source of quinine, the first effective antimalarial. 'Jesuit's bark' was stashed aboard colonial navies and gave us tonic water and gin and tonic.

entries.name: Sweet wormwood
entries.spread: Mawangdui silk texts c. 168 BCE mention it for fevers; Project 523 in 1969 isolated artemisinin; now the backbone of malaria treatment worldwide
needs: harvested at peak bloom for artemisinin content
entries.notes: Source of artemisinin, which won the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Killed more malaria parasites in the last 50 years than any other drug.

entries.name: Foxglove

domesticated.where: western Europe; cultivated, not truly domesticated

entries.spread: William Withering, 1785: dropsy and the foxglove; digitalis standardised a century later; the basis of modern digoxin for heart failure
needs: biennial: leaves from year one, flowers year two
entries.notes: Every part of the plant is poisonous; the leaf makes the medicine. Cardiac glycosides slow and strengthen the failing heart - dose separates cure from death.

entries.name: Madagascar periwinkle
entries.spread: Global ornamental before 1958; Eli Lilly trials revealed vinblastine and vincristine; now a frontline chemotherapy plant
needs: grows as a small perennial herb
entries.notes: A garden pink in most suburbs whose alkaloids treat childhood leukaemia and Hodgkin's lymphoma. The classic story of screening wild plants for drugs.

entries.name: Asian ginseng
entries.spread: Chinese materia medica since the Han dynasty; Korean red ginseng trade; cultivated US ginseng in Appalachia for the export market
entries.notes: Slow-growing obligate-shade root worth more per kilogram than most crops except truffles. Wild roots fetch astronomical prices and are largely poached to extinction.

entries.name: Pyrethrum

domesticated.where: Dalmatia; modern plantations in Kenya and Tanzania from the 19th century

entries.spread: Crushed Dalmatian flea powder in the 1800s; Kenya and Tanzania lead exports; the model for all modern synthetic pyrethroids
needs: flowers picked, dried and milled for pyrethrins
entries.notes: A daisy-like composite whose flower heads yield six natural insecticides. Non-toxic to mammals at use rates; bees are collateral damage.
